newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss shares end lower after 10-day record run.
newsitem.headline: Swiss shares end lower after 10-day record run.

text.p: 1530 GMT - The Swiss bourse's ten-day run of record closings ended on Friday as profit taking pulled shares down from an early all-time high of 4,467.4 points on the Swiss Market Index (SMI).
Dealers welcomed the correction, saying it was not expected to dampen overall favourable sentiment. One trader added that buying regularly sets in once prices start to slip.
* Blue-chip SMI lost 7.8 points, or 0.18 percent, to 4,436.3 points.
* All-share Swiss Performance Index (SPI) ended down 1.95 points, or 0.07 percent, to 2,824.34 points.
Traders said some investors were disappointed that Wall Street gains and the firming U.S. dollar did not give a stronger sustained boost to Swiss shares.
* Roche certificates, which saw buying interest for most of the session, ended five francs down at 12,465. The stock reached an all-time high of 12,695 francs in early trade.
* Novartis registereds fell two francs to 1,740.
* Among major banks and insurers, Winterthur stood out with an advance of seven francs to 872. UBS added two francs to 1,277 francs. CS Holding, SBC, Zurich, Swiss Re and Baloise were lower.

* Industrials Electrowatt, Holderbank and Sulzer were slightly higher. ABB gave up 15 francs to 1,830. Alusuisse slid 20 francs to 1,157. Dealers said that some investors, who had hoped the company would announce a spin-off at Tuesday's press conference, sold the stock. SMH bearers slumped 15 francs to 938.
* Swissair gave up five francs to 1,335.
* Adecco stocks ended up 5.50 francs to 441.

* On the Swiss Options and Futures Exchange (Soffex), demand was high once again for SMI options and futures, although volume did not reach Wednesday's levels. 73,752 SMI option and 7,160 SMI futures changed hands. Total volume stood at 156,210 contracts and the call put ratio was 1.32 to one.

Dealers said hedging activity increased after prices on the share market ceased to rise. But the fact that there were more calls than puts showed that a majority of market players were optimistic, they said.
